sharedOptions.text: The plants on the other side of the room were not touched at all.
Nearby plants are able to pick up this warning from the air.
Insects will disappear from a field once the plants warn each other.
Science is only beginning to translate their chemical language.
Early trials show that such fields need far less pesticide.
Gardeners should water their plants early in the morning.
Something surprising happens to the plants growing beside it.

segments.text: When insects attack a plant, the plant does not stay silent.

Scientists discovered that the injured plant sends chemicals into the air, warning its neighbours of danger.

In one classic experiment, researchers put two groups of plants in the same room and let caterpillars eat the leaves of one group.

Days later, however, those healthy plants had produced a bitter substance that made their leaves hard to digest.

The chemical message works like a school bell.

As soon as a neighbouring plant 'smells' the warning in the air, it begins producing its own bitter chemicals, even though no insect has touched it yet. This early preparation explains why some fields suffer less damage during insect outbreaks than others.

Farmers are now testing how to use this natural system. Some spray a safe chemical that imitates the warning signal, and the whole field prepares itself for attack.

In the future, crops may be protected not by stronger poisons but by better communication.

There is still much to learn. Plants have no ears or eyes, yet they clearly sense the world around them.
The quiet conversations in a field remind us that even the stillness of nature is full of activity.
